n: In this lecture we will study forensic chemical objects and the procedure for working with physical evidence. The outline: forensic chemical objects; taking, preserving and sending them; reception and storage; preliminary examination, that is, pH, colour and odour. Key terms: physical evidence, biological object, preservation, report, preliminary examination and presumptive reaction. Forensic chemical investigation is mainly the examination of physical evidence. In many cases it is an irreplaceable object, so caution and economy are required.

The objects of chemical-toxicological analysis are divided into three groups. The first is the biological object: the general name for organs of a corpse, blood, urine, vomit and gastric lavage fluids. The second is products and the environment: foodstuffs, water, medicines, air. The third is articles: clothing, stains, vessels. Depending on the type of object, the method of isolation differs: alkaloids are isolated differently from organs, urine and plants. A poison is often present in a very small amount, so it is first isolated and then identified by a reaction.

t: Standard A-6: Principles of Taking Objects
n: Standard A-6 sets out the principles of taking objects. Internal organs, blood and urine are submitted. In selecting them, the nature of the poison, its route of entry, distribution, route and rate of elimination, duration of intoxication and therapeutic measures are taken into account. Vomit, the first portion of the lavage fluid, chemical and medicinal substances, food and drinks are also submitted. Objects are submitted in sufficient quantity, taking into account that one third remains in the archive for repeat examination. That is, two thirds of the submitted objects are used, and one third is kept in the department archive for repeat analysis.

t: Objects Taken When Poisoning Is Suspected
n: When poisoning is suspected, a complex of internal organs is taken. It includes the stomach contents, one third of the liver, bile and one kidney. In addition, urine up to 200 ml and 200 ml of blood are taken. Each organ, the blood and the urine are placed in a separate clean, dry glass jar. If particles, crystals or tablets are found in the stomach contents, they too are sent for forensic chemical examination.

t: Additional Objects by Route of Entry
n: Additional objects are taken depending on the route of entry. If the route of entry of the poison is suspected, an additional sample is taken from the corresponding site. Look at the table: when entry is through the vagina or uterus, the vagina and uterus are taken in separate vessels. For subcutaneous or intramuscular entry, the skin and muscles of the suspected area are taken. In inhalation poisoning, that is, through breathing, 300 g each of a lung portion from the most blood-filled area and the brain are taken.

When ethanol or narcotic substances are suspected, the objects differ. For ethanol, blood and urine are taken, 10-20 ml each, in a vessel filled to the stopper. Blood is taken from large veins or from the sinuses of the dura mater with a pipette or syringe. If blood and urine cannot be submitted, about 100 g of muscle tissue is submitted. For narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances, blood 150 ml, urine 150-200 ml and the gallbladder are always taken. Remember: in ethyl alcohol poisoning, a delay in sending the materials may lead to unreliable results in quantitative determination.

t: Acids, Organochlorine Substances and Methyl Alcohol
n: The objects for acids, organochlorine substances and methyl alcohol are as follows. For acids and alkalis, the larynx, trachea, oesophagus, stomach wall and skin exposed to the poison are taken. Organochlorines include chloroform, chloral hydrate, carbon tetrachloride, dichloroethane and pesticides; for these, 200 g of brain is taken. For methyl alcohol, brain, liver and kidney 100 g each are taken, and blood and urine 10-20 ml each. In the table, for organochlorines, the omentum, brain, blood, urine, liver and kidney are indicated.

Requirements for glycosides, organophosphorus compounds and carbon monoxide. For glycosides, one third of the liver with the gallbladder is taken; because they decompose rapidly, the tissues of the injection area are submitted preserved in ethyl alcohol. For organophosphorus compounds, liver, kidney, urine, stomach, intestine and blood are taken; the blood is needed to determine cholinesterase activity. For carbon monoxide, blood is taken, 10-20 ml.

Metallic poisons, methaemoglobin and plant poisons. For mercury salts, hair, nails, liver and kidney are taken. In chronic lead, thallium and arsenic poisoning, hair, nails, flat bones, liver and kidney are taken. For poisons that form methaemoglobin, that is, ferrocyanides, aniline, nitrobenzene, potassium permanganate, formaldehyde, chromates, methylene blue and acetaldehyde, blood is taken in order to determine methaemoglobin. For mushrooms and poisonous plants, undigested fragments, vomit and lavage fluids are submitted.

There are four rules for removing organs. The contents of the oesophagus, stomach and intestine are removed after two ligatures have been applied, so that they do not mix mechanically. Internal organs must not be washed with water or contaminated with chemicals or mechanical impurities. Organs are placed in dry wide-mouthed glass jars. The use of metal or ceramic vessels is prohibited. Remember: applying two ligatures prevents the substances from mixing with one another, and not washing with water helps avoid losing the poison.

Expert supervision and preparation of vessels. The expert must ensure that the poisonous substance does not escape from the corpse and does not get in from outside. Before the corpse is opened, the autopsy table, instruments and gloves are washed thoroughly; during the examination, water and other liquids are not used. The jars are washed with a soda or mustard solution, rinsed with clean water and then with distilled water, and dried in a drying cabinet.

Rules of preservation. On hot days, if the object is to be sent far away, ethyl alcohol is used as the preservative. If it is recommended that the object be tested for ethyl alcohol and nitrite, preservation with ethyl alcohol is prohibited. A sample of the ethyl alcohol must be sent to the laboratory together with the preserved object. Under Standard A-6, preservation is carried out only when cardiac glycosides are suspected; the ethyl alcohol covers the object by at least 1 cm, and a 300 ml sample of alcohol is sent.

The dispatch procedure consists of several stages. The jar containing the biological object is closed tightly and a wax seal is applied. On the label are written the deceased's first name and surname, year of birth, name of the organ, number of the forensic medical examination report and the serial number of the jar. The jars are closed tightly, a label is attached, and they are placed in a sealed polyethylene bag or container and sent. Together with the object, the referral of the forensic medical expert or the ruling of the investigative and judicial bodies ordering the examination is sent.

Let us dwell on the objects taken from an exhumed corpse. In exhumation, 500 g of soil is submitted from six places, that is, above and below the coffin, from the sides, and from the head and foot ends. Pieces of clothing, and of upholstery and lining fabrics, are submitted. The bottom board of the coffin, about 500 cubic cm, and jewellery and other items found beside the corpse are also sent. In the table the objects are given briefly: soil from 6 places, 500 g each; coffin board, 500 cubic cm; fabrics as clothing and upholstery; also jewellery and so on.

Rules for receiving physical evidence. Physical evidence must be wrapped and sealed by the body that ordered the examination and listed in the accompanying documents. If the packaging is improper, or if it was sent from the city in which the forensic medical department is located, the physical evidence is not accepted and is returned. Physical evidence and the documents relating to it are registered in a special log of the department. Organic solvents, acids, alkalis, hydrocyanic acid, cocaine and similar substances are volatile and decompose rapidly. Therefore the examination must begin on the day of receipt.

On receipt, the expert chemist carefully inspects the packaging of the item and describes it. The following are noted: the type of binding and whether it can be removed without breaking the seal; the dimensions of the box, packet or jar; the condition of the inscriptions and seal, that is, intact or broken; defects in the packaging. The packaging is opened very carefully so as not to damage the vessel or lose the objects. Careful opening of the vessel's packaging is the very first condition of correct analysis.

The next step: the inscriptions on the vessel are compared with the accompanying documents. If there is a discrepancy between the inscriptions and the documents, the analysis results may be wrong. In such cases a report is drawn up with a three-member panel present, and other evidence is requested from the judicial bodies or the forensic medical laboratory. In the practical class, the packaging and integrity of the objects, the medium, colour and consistency are studied.

t: Storage of Physical Evidence and Documents
n: Rules for storing physical evidence and documents. Physical evidence is kept in a separate lockable, sealable cabinet; perishable objects in a refrigerator, which is likewise locked and sealed. Documents delivered with the physical evidence are kept in a separate folder, in a safe or a lockable cabinet. Objects liable to putrefaction, if they cannot be returned, are kept preserved in ethyl alcohol in the refrigerator for one year, then destroyed in the prescribed manner. Objects submitted for the determination of ethyl alcohol are destroyed 30 days after the investigation is complete.

Analysis is divided into full and incomplete types. Depending on the task set before the expert chemist, analysis is divided into full and incomplete. In an incomplete analysis, the expert, on special instruction, tests for one or several poisonous substances. In a full analysis, the expert chemist is required to test for 67 poisonous substances. The difference is that an incomplete analysis depends on the instruction, whereas a full analysis is carried out according to a set list.

t: Full Analysis: Volatile and Metallic Poisons
n: In a full analysis, volatile and metallic poisons make up two groups of 13 each. There are 13 volatile poisons: hydrocyanic acid and its compounds; methyl, ethyl, propyl, butyl, amyl and isoamyl alcohols; formaldehyde; chloroform; chloral hydrate; carbon tetrachloride; dichloroethane; phenol and cresols. Metal-containing poisons number 13 in all: salts of barium, manganese, chromium, zinc, thallium, lead, copper, mercury, bismuth, cadmium, silver, arsenic and antimony. Order No. 551 of the Ministry of Health of Uzbekistan states that in a full examination 13 volatile substances must be tested for; they are isolated by distillation methods.

t: Poisons Isolated by the Acidified Method
n: Poisons isolated by the acidified water and alcohol method comprise three groups: 7 barbiturates, 14 alkaloids and 7 synthetic substances. Barbiturates: barbital, phenobarbital, barbamyl, etaminal, cyclobarbital, hexobarbital, that is, evipan, and benzonal. The list continues: morphine, codeine, dionine, heroin, hydrocodone, papaverine, promedol. Further: strychnine, atropine, hyoscyamine, scopolamine, cocaine, pachycarpine, anabasine and nicotine. Synthetic substances: aminazine, diprazine, tisercin, mazheptil, triftazine, imizine and its analogues. That is, barbiturates, alkaloids and synthetic substances together belong to this group, and all of them are isolated by the acidified water and alcohol method.

t: Poisons Isolated with an Organic Solvent
n: Poisons isolated by infusion with an organic solvent: karbofos, metafos, methylethylthiophos. Also methylnitrophos, trichlormetafos, fozalon, butifos, chlorophos, phthalophos, octamethyl and sevin. This group includes pesticides, cardiac glycosides and others. Chlorophos is isolated by steam distillation, by acidified water and alcohol, and by infusion with ether. Thus one substance can be isolated by several methods, and among the poisons isolated with an organic solvent, pesticides and cardiac glycosides hold a special place.

The chemical-toxicological investigation consists of several stages: isolation, purification from foreign substances, and qualitative and quantitative determination. The chain is as follows: isolation from the object, purification of the solution, qualitative determination, then quantitative determination. Chemical, physical and physicochemical methods are used at the stages. The result of isolation is a liquid: a distillate, mineralisate or dialysate. This liquid is purified at the following stages, and the substance is determined from it qualitatively and quantitatively.

There are four main methods of isolating poisons. Extraction is the main method of isolation from blood, urine and lavage fluids: substances dissolved in water are extracted with an organic solvent immiscible with water. Steam distillation is used for hydrocyanic acid, alcohols, formaldehyde, hexachlorane and nicotine. Vacuum distillation is carried out at low pressure and low temperature; it is suitable for substances that decompose on heating, for example TEL, that is, tetraethyl lead. Metallic poisons are isolated by wet or dry mineralisation, that is, destruction methods.

Extraction is the redistribution of a substance dissolved in one solvent between two immiscible liquids, that is, water and an organic solvent. Partition continues until the concentration of the substance is equalised in both solvents; the insolubility of foreign substances, protein, fat and pigments is important. The nature of the solvent, the pH of the medium and electrolytes strongly affect solubility. The partition coefficient is expressed by the formula K = C(org) / C(water): it must be greater than one for a substance dissolved in the organic solvent, and less than one for a substance dissolved in water.

There are five methods of purifying isolates. Saponification is used for compounds resistant to hydrolysis; for example, in purifying organochlorine compounds from fat, the fat is hydrolysed. In re-extraction, solubility changes with a change in pH: substances of acidic character dissolve well in water under alkaline conditions, and alkaloids dissolve well in an organic solvent. Sulphonation is used for extracts rich in fat and lipids, for substances resistant to concentrated sulphuric acid, for example barbiturates. Chromatographic methods, thin-layer and gas-liquid, are more widely used; fats and waxy substances are precipitated with acetone and acetonitrile in the cold.

Poisons are divided into groups according to the method of isolation, first groups 1-3. The first group is volatile poisons: hydrocyanic and acetic acid, poisonous halogen compounds, alcohols, aldehydes, phenols; they are isolated by steam distillation. The second group is isolated by the acidified method: barbiturates, alkaloids, their analogues and nitrogen-containing synthetic compounds, with the help of acidic water and alcohol. The third group is metallic poisons: heavy metals and arsenic, by mineralisation, that is, by incineration.

t: Classification of Poisons: Groups 4-6 and Choice of Method
n: Now groups 4-6. The fourth group is dialysis: mineral acids, alkalis and salts are isolated by soaking with water and dialysis. The fifth group, by infusion with an organic solvent, isolates pesticides and cardiac glycosides. The sixth group is special methods: TEL, zinc phosphide, fluorides. Chloral hydrate and phenol are isolated not only by distillation but also by other methods. Liquid alkaloids can be isolated by acidified water and alcohol as well as by distillation. On the basis of physicochemical properties, the results are compared and the method by which the most substance was isolated is chosen.

t: Preliminary Examination and the Investigation Plan
n: On the preliminary examination and the investigation plan. There are very many substances that cause poisoning, so testing every object for every poison would take a great deal of time. To save the object and to save time, the forensic chemist draws up a clear plan. The preliminary examination makes it possible to rule out or suggest many substances within the plan. The bases of the plan: referrals and causes of death, the case history and the forensic medical examination report, as well as the appearance of the object, that is, pH, odour, colour, and the results of the preliminary presumptive testing.

The stages of the preliminary examination are carried out in sequence. First the packaging of the vessel is opened carefully, and the inscriptions are compared with the documents. Then the appearance, consistency and morphological structure are examined, the colour, odour and foreign matter are determined, and then pH is measured with an indicator. Consistency and morphological structure help to decide the method of isolation and to name the organs precisely. Remember: the preliminary chemical examination does not identify the poison completely, but it determines what is to be identified first.

Foreign inclusions and odour also give preliminary information. With the eye or under a microscope, inclusions characteristic of a poison may be visible: porcelain-like crystals of arsenic oxide, prismatic crystals of strychnine nitrate, seeds of poisonous plants. A foreign admixture is picked out with tweezers and tested for the suspected substance. The odour of bitter almonds is characteristic of cyanides; the odour of pyridine bases is characteristic of poisoning with denatured alcohol; organophosphorus compounds also have a distinctive odour. The odour is well perceived if the object has not putrefied; because of putrefaction products, the odour of poisonous substances changes.

t: Colour of the Object and Coloured Inclusions
n: The colour of the object also gives direction. A yellow colour is characteristic of poisoning with picric acid, strychnine, chromates or nitric acid; black, of sulphuric acid. Coloured inclusions: concentrated sulphuric, nitric and picric acids, acrichin, Schweinfurt green. If the object contains foreign crystalline substances, plant parts or fruit remnants, the chemist first studies their character and obtains a pointer to the poison. Standing for a long time before analysis begins, and putrefaction, interfere with identifying characteristic odours.

t: Determining and Interpreting the pH of the Medium
n: The procedure for determining and interpreting the pH of the medium. The object is mixed with 0.5-1.0 ml of water; after 3-5 minutes it is dropped onto indicator paper. If the pH is 3 or lower, this mainly indicates the presence of mineral or many organic acids. A weakly acidic medium indicates fermentation; in an alkaline medium, testing for alkalis or carbonates is carried out. The table gives the indicator ranges: litmus 5.0-8.0, Congo red 3.0-5.2, phenolphthalein 8.2-10.0.

Presumptive methods are assessed in terms of sensitivity and specificity. Some presumptive methods, although highly sensitive, are not specific; owing to their sensitivity they can detect even a substance at a therapeutic dose. If the presumptive test is positive, the necessary main examination for the suspected substances must be carried out. In presumptive testing, microdiffusion, microcrystalloscopic reactions and chromatographic screening methods are mainly used. Example: phenothiazine derivatives give a light red colour when a solution of ferric chloride in sulphuric acid is added to urine. For barbiturates, cobalt acetate is used under ammonia or lithium hydroxide conditions.

The preliminary test for white arsenic is carried out in five stages. First stage: an inclusion in the object in the form of a piece of porcelain is picked out with tweezers. Second: it is placed in a thin glass test tube, a small piece of charcoal is added, and it is heated over a weak flame; before heating, the upper part of the tube is wrapped with paper or gauze moistened with purified water. Result: if, on unwrapping the moistened part, there is a dark grey spot on the wall, this indicates the presence of white arsenic. For confirmation, the tip of the tube is broken off, the place of the dark spot is heated, and another place is cooled; a white spot forms at the cooled place.

The procedure for the preliminary test for hydrocyanic acid. A small piece of the object is placed in a small porcelain dish and oxalic acid is added. A microscope slide with a drop of alkali solution on its underside is placed over it, and it is left for a while. The slide is removed gently, one drop of a mixture of FeCl3 and FeCl2 salts is dropped onto it, and hydrochloric acid is added. If hydrocyanic acid is present, a blue colour forms.

t: Preliminary Tests for Nitrite, Nitrate and Aminazine
n: Preliminary tests for nitrite, nitrate and aminazine. Nitrates and nitrites: a piece of the object is soaked in water, diphenylamine reagent and concentrated sulphuric acid are added to the aqueous solution, and a blue colour results. If the result is positive, the azo dye reaction is carried out: when a mixture of hydrochloric and sulphanilic acids and an alkaline solution of naphthol are added, a red dye forms. Aminazine in urine: if 1 ml of reagent, that is, 80 ml of 10% H2SO4 + 20 ml of 5% FeCl3, is added to 1 ml of urine, a red-pink colour appears. Or if 1 ml of FPN reagent, that is, 5 ml of 5% FeCl3; 45 ml of 20% HClO4; 50 ml of 50% HNO3, is added to 1 ml of urine, a red colour forms.

Let us conclude the topic. Physical evidence is in many cases an irreplaceable object: the examination is carried out carefully and on the basis of a clear plan. Objects are taken according to the nature of the poison and the route of entry, and are sent sealed in glass vessels; one third remains in the archive. The preliminary examination, that is, appearance, colour, odour, pH and foreign inclusions, gives a pointer for drawing up the plan, but is not a final conclusion. According to the method of isolation, poisons are divided into 6 groups: volatile, acidified, mineralisation, dialysis, organic solvent and special methods.
